mainTopicBrief: 本单元围绕“为瘦而伤”的新闻事件，涵盖科学健身与饮食（Reading）、身材焦虑与自我接纳（Extended reading）和理性看待整容（Integrated skills）三个子话题——健康类命题在高考应用文与雅思议论文中都属必练靶区。

subTopics.title: 科学减肥与健康生活
subTopics.desc: 课文新闻：Jennifer 因节食晕倒——so-called 'quick-fix methods' 有害，balanced diet + regular exercise 才是正道。

prompts.task: 假设你是李华。你的美国笔友 Lisa 来信说她为了快速减肥经常不吃早餐（skip breakfast），最近上课很难集中注意力。请你写一封回信，内容包括：1. 表达关心；2. 指出这种做法的危害；3. 提出健康建议。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
Dear Lisa,

I'm worried to learn that you often skip breakfast to lose weight and now have trouble concentrating in class.

Please stop — these so-called "quick-fix methods" prove to be harmful. Skipping meals leads to dangerously low blood sugar levels, which explains your tiredness. In the news, a teenager even fainted after skipping meals; habits like these, if maintained over the long term, can become a serious health risk.

Here is my advice. Have a healthy, well-balanced diet, and never trade meals for a number on the scale. Besides, take regular exercise — aim for the daily average of 30 to 60 minutes — and keep regular hours. In time you will get into shape and feel energetic again.

Yours,
Li Hua

prompts.task: 阅读下面短文，根据所给情节和段落开头语进行续写，使之构成一个完整的故事。续写词数应为150左右。
prompts.storyContext: To lose weight before the school sports meet, Jenny had been skipping meals for a whole week. She was proud of the number on the scales, but she felt weak and dizzy, and could barely concentrate in class. Her best friend warned her to eat properly, but Jenny insisted she was fine.
prompts.para1: Paragraph 1: During the morning run, Jenny suddenly felt the world spin and had to sit down.
prompts.para2: Paragraph 2: From that day, Jenny threw away her crash-diet plan for good.
prompts.reference:
During the morning run, Jenny suddenly felt the world spin and had to sit down. Her vision blurred, her legs gave way, and the next thing she knew, the school doctor was holding a cup of sugar water to her lips. "Your blood sugar is dangerously low," the doctor said gently. "Starving yourself is not losing weight — it is hurting your body." Lying there, pale and shaking, Jenny felt frightened and ashamed.

From that day, Jenny threw away her crash-diet plan for good. With the doctor's help, she learned to eat a well-balanced diet and to exercise sensibly instead of starving. Slowly her energy returned, her mind grew sharper, and — to her surprise — she felt fitter than ever on sports day. Real health, she finally understood, is grown day by day, not starved overnight.

prompts.task: An increasing number of teenagers are trying to lose weight in unhealthy ways. What are the causes of this trend? What solutions can you suggest? (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
In many countries, growing numbers of teenagers are starving themselves, over-exercising or taking diet pills in pursuit of a thinner body. Explaining this worrying trend, and finding ways to reverse it, deserves serious attention.

The causes lie chiefly in the images young people absorb. In a culture where being thin is routinely presented as being beautiful, the media parade flawless bodies as the price of admission to happiness, and social platforms turn appearance into a daily competition scored in likes. Teenagers, whose self-image is still under construction, are especially defenceless against this message. A second cause is ignorance: many genuinely believe that skipping meals is a shortcut, unaware that so-called quick-fix methods slow the body down, damage concentration and, maintained over time, become a serious health risk.

Solutions should therefore target both the message and the knowledge gap. Schools can teach media literacy alongside biology, showing students how images are edited and how starvation actually undermines the slimness it promises. Health classes ought to replace vague warnings with practical guidance — balanced meals, regular exercise and sufficient sleep — so that the healthy route is as concrete as the harmful one. Parents and doctors, for their part, should watch for warning signs and respond with support rather than criticism, since shame is precisely what drives secret dieting.

No single measure will dissolve a pressure that flows from the surrounding culture. But when young people understand both why the images lie and how real fitness is built, the appeal of dangerous shortcuts fades — and health, not thinness, becomes the goal worth chasing.

subTopics.title: 健康生活方式
subTopics.desc: 本单元主题延伸：拒绝 quick-fix methods，用 a well-balanced diet 与 regular exercise 打好健康的地基——好身材不是饿出来的，是养出来的。

prompts.task: 你的英国朋友 Sam 最近想通过节食快速减肥。请你用英文回信，劝他采取健康的生活方式，内容包括：1. 表达关心；2. 指出节食的危害；3. 提出健康建议。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
Dear Sam,

I was a little worried to hear that you are trying to lose weight quickly by skipping meals. As a friend, I really hope you will think twice.

Quick-fix methods may work for a few days, but they often do more harm than good. When you skip meals, your blood sugar drops, and you may have trouble concentrating in class. Crash diets rarely last, and the weight usually comes back.

Why not build a healthy lifestyle instead? Eat a well-balanced diet with plenty of vegetables, drink enough water, and take regular exercise such as running or basketball. Good shape is not starved into being; it is grown, day by day.

Take care of yourself!

Yours,
Li Hua
vocabHints: lose weight quickly by skipping meals

prompts.storyContext: After weeks of late nights, endless screens and junk food, Mark realised he could barely climb the stairs to his classroom without panting. His eyes were tired, his mind was foggy, and he had no energy for anything. Something, he knew, had to change — and it had to change soon.

prompts.para2: Paragraph 2: A month later, the boy who once gasped on the stairs ran up them two at a time.
prompts.reference:
That weekend, Mark drew up a simple plan and pinned it above his desk. It was nothing dramatic: sleep by eleven, a short run every morning, more vegetables and less soda, and no phone one hour before bed. The first few days were hard, and more than once he wanted to give up. But he crossed off each day on his chart, and slowly the new habits began to feel natural.

A month later, the boy who once gasped on the stairs ran up them two at a time. His eyes were brighter, his mind was clearer, and he could focus in class as never before. Friends asked him for his secret, expecting some magic trick, but Mark only smiled and pointed at the little chart on his wall. Good health, he had learned, is built one small, steady day at a time.

prompts.task: Some people believe that individuals are responsible for their own health and fitness, while others think governments should do more to keep people healthy. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
As rates of obesity and lifestyle-related illness climb, societies argue over who should be blamed and who should act. Some insist that health is a matter of personal choice; others hold governments responsible. In my view both share the duty, though individuals must own the daily decisions while governments shape the environment around them.

The case for personal responsibility is strong. No official can force anyone to eat sensibly, exercise or sleep well; these are private acts repeated every day, and adults who ignore obvious advice can hardly blame the state for the consequences. Treating people as helpless also insults their dignity and, taken far enough, invites endless interference in private life.

Yet individual willpower operates within conditions that governments largely control. When cities lack parks and safe paths, when cheap food is engineered to be fattening, and when advertising floods children with junk, poor 'choices' become predictable outcomes rather than free decisions. Governments can tilt these conditions toward health — taxing sugary drinks, funding sports facilities, regulating misleading labels and teaching nutrition in schools — measures that have measurably improved public health where applied.

The sensible conclusion is therefore partnership rather than blame. People should be expected to look after themselves, but they can only do so easily if the healthy option is also the affordable and convenient one, and creating that environment is a job only governments can perform.

In conclusion, health is neither purely a private duty nor purely a public one. Lasting improvement comes when responsible individuals are supported by a society deliberately designed to make healthy living the natural choice.

subTopics.title: 理性看待整容
subTopics.desc: 课文新闻双案例：烧伤修复的 Mr Wilson vs 不满外貌的 Miss Edwards——weigh up all of the advantages and disadvantages, think before you act。

prompts.task: 你班将举行以 "Should Teenagers Have Cosmetic Surgery?" 为主题的英语讨论会。请你准备一篇发言稿表明你的观点，内容包括：1. 你的观点；2. 两条理由；3. 建议。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
Good afternoon, everyone!

Should teenagers have cosmetic surgery just to look better? My answer is no — at least not before we grow up.

First, our bodies are still growing, so the results might not be what we expect; some people even end up looking unnatural, unable to make certain facial expressions. Second, surgery cannot cure the real problem, which often lies in confidence rather than appearance. True beauty, as we all know, comes from what we do and who we are.

Of course, surgery that treats burns or injuries is a different matter. But before making any decision, we must weigh up all of the advantages and disadvantages. Think before you act!

Thank you!
vocabHints: the results might not be what people expect
weigh up the advantages and disadvantages

prompts.storyContext: Ever since she started following a beauty influencer online, Lily had been begging her mother to let her change her face — a smaller nose, a sharper chin, 'just like the photos'. She was convinced that only then would she finally feel pretty. Her mother listened quietly but said nothing at first.
prompts.para1: Paragraph 1: Her grandmother, hearing about the plan, quietly took out an old photo album.
prompts.para2: Paragraph 2: Turning the last page, Lily suddenly saw her own face in a new light.
prompts.reference:
Her grandmother, hearing about the plan, quietly took out an old photo album. Page by page, she showed Lily faces from three generations — her great-grandmother's warm smile, her mother's bright eyes, her own dimpled cheeks as a child. "Look," Grandma said softly, "you carry all of us in your face. These are not flaws; they are our family's story." Lily had never thought of it that way before.

Turning the last page, Lily suddenly saw her own face in a new light. The nose she had wanted to change was her mother's; the smile was her grandmother's. Filtered photos online suddenly seemed hollow beside the living history in her own reflection. Lily quietly closed the album and hugged her grandmother. "Maybe," she whispered, "I'll keep the face I was given." And for the first time, she truly meant it.
vocabHints: not flaws but our family's story

prompts.task: More and more young people are choosing to have cosmetic surgery to improve their appearance. Do you think this is a positive or negative development? (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
Cosmetic procedures, once the preserve of the wealthy few, are now marketed to ordinary young people as casually as a new hairstyle. Whether this normalisation is welcome is open to debate; in my view, it is a largely negative development, with one clearly positive exception.

The exception deserves stating first. Reconstructive surgery — repairing skin after burns, correcting features damaged by accident or illness — restores what misfortune took away, and the confidence it returns to a patient is beyond argument. A man who can face the world again after a fire owes modern medicine a genuine debt.

Elective surgery on healthy young faces is another matter. Medically, a body that is still developing makes a poor canvas: results shift as growth continues, and some patients end up with faces that look unnatural or move unwillingly. Psychologically, the knife treats the symptom while feeding the disease. Dissatisfaction with one's appearance usually grows from comparison and insecurity; each operation confirms the belief that the fault lay in the face rather than in the standard it was measured against. It is telling that satisfaction after such procedures is often brief, with attention simply migrating to the next perceived flaw. Socially, every normalised operation raises the price of remaining natural, quietly pressuring peers to follow.

I do not argue for prohibition; adults are entitled to their choices. But a culture that teaches its youngest members to correct their faces before their characters have finished forming has confused the order of self-improvement. On balance, the trend does more harm than good.

prompts.task: 你校英文报正举办以 "Learning to Like Myself" 为主题的征文活动。请你写一篇短文投稿，内容包括：1. 你或身边人曾有的外貌焦虑；2. 转变的经过；3. 你的感悟。注意：词数100左右。
prompts.reference:
For a long time, dark thoughts about my ordinary looks hung over me. Comparing myself with the perfect faces online, I only ended up feeling worse about myself.

The turning point came when my art teacher praised my sketches in front of the class. For the first time, I realized that everyone has their own talents, and that trying to live up to the standards of beauty in the media is fighting a losing battle.

Now I take pride in the things I do well. My contents, I have learned, are far more important than my cover. Like what you do, and you will learn to like who you are.

prompts.storyContext: Ever since a classmate joked that she was 'the tallest girl in the class', Cindy had hated her own height. She began to slouch, to stand at the back, to wish she could disappear. Whenever she passed a mirror, she saw only what she believed was wrong with her.

prompts.para2: Paragraph 2: When the photo came out, Cindy looked at it and, for the first time, smiled at herself.
prompts.reference:
Before the class photo, Cindy tried to hide herself at the very back of the group, bending her knees so she would look shorter. But the photographer called out kindly, "Tall girl in the middle, please — you'll balance the picture perfectly!" Reluctantly, Cindy stepped forward and stood up straight. To her surprise, her teacher whispered, "You have such a graceful posture when you don't hide it."

When the photo came out, Cindy looked at it and, for the first time, smiled at herself. There she was, standing tall in the centre, and she did not look strange at all — she looked confident, even beautiful. She realised that her height had never been the problem; hiding from it had. From that day, Cindy walked with her head held high, comfortable at last in her own skin.

prompts.task: Advertising and social media promote unrealistic standards of physical beauty. Some people think this has a harmful effect on young people. To what extent do you agree or disagree? (Write at least 250 words.)
prompts.reference:
Modern advertising and social media surround young people with images of physical perfection that few real bodies can match. It is widely argued that this stream of idealised beauty does genuine harm to the young, and I agree almost without reservation.

The central harm is a quiet redefinition of normal. When every billboard face is flawless and every feed is filtered, the ordinary body — the kind most people actually inhabit — begins to look like a failure. Teenagers, still assembling their identities, absorb this arithmetic quickly: they compare, find themselves lacking, and end up feeling worse about a self that was never defective in the first place. The consequences are not merely emotional. Chasing an unreachable standard pushes some towards punishing diets and obsessive exercise, a battle that cannot be won because the finish line is imaginary; others withdraw socially, convinced that their worth is measured in their reflection.

Defenders of the industry reply that such images are aspiration, not instruction, and that beauty content can motivate healthy habits. The argument fails on one decisive point: the standards promoted are not honestly labelled as constructed. A photograph edited beyond reality is presented as reality, and young viewers are invited to judge their unedited selves against it — a comparison rigged from the start.

I would allow one small qualification: the harm is not evenly distributed, and confident teenagers with strong offline lives often shrug the images off. Yet policy cannot be built on the resilient few. Until idealised images carry honest labels, their net effect on the young remains, in my judgement, plainly harmful.
